title: SAM, references, defaults, receivers
scopeHtml: Scope: SAM conversions and fun interface, Java SAM interop, function and bound references, lambdas with receiver as a concept, default and named arguments, @JvmOverloads basics, vararg and spread, local functions, tailrec, operator invoke, plus production scenarios on leaks, crossinline Runnables, inline bloat and default-argument ABI breaks. (Inline mechanics, lambda bytecode and crossinline rules live in K3a. DSL builders live in K9.)

questions.promptHtml: What is a SAM conversion, and why does a plain Kotlin interface with one method not accept a lambda unless you mark it fun interface?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know the difference between function types and nominal interfaces, and whether you can design a callback API that works for Kotlin and Java callers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SAM means Single Abstract Method. A SAM conversion lets me pass a lambda where an interface with exactly one abstract method is expected. The compiler builds an instance of that interface whose method runs the lambda body. Java interfaces always get this, because Java has no function types. Kotlin interfaces only get it if I declare them fun interface, which arrived in Kotlin 1.4. Kotlin makes it opt-in because it already has function types, and turning every one-method interface into a lambda target would quietly lock that interface into a public contract: adding a second abstract method later would break every lambda call site.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Kotlin has two ways to express "a piece of behaviour":
    • A function type (Int) -> Boolean. It is structural: any lambda with a matching shape fits. On the JVM it is a kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<Integer, Boolean>.
    • A nominal interface interface IntPredicate { fun accept(i: Int): Boolean }. It is its own named type with its own name, KDoc, extension functions and identity.
  • A SAM conversion bridges the two. When the expected type is a functional interface, the compiler accepts a lambda or a callable reference and produces an interface instance.
  • Rules for fun interface:
    • It must have exactly one abstract member function.
    • It may have any number of non-abstract members (methods with bodies) and may extend other interfaces, as long as the total count of abstract functions stays at one.
    • It cannot have abstract properties.
  • Java interfaces with one abstract method get conversions automatically. Methods inherited from Object such as equals do not count toward the "one abstract method" total. Since Kotlin 1.4 the conversion also works when a Kotlin function takes a Java SAM parameter. Before 1.4 it only applied to calls into Java methods.
  • Compilation: since Kotlin 1.5, SAM conversions on JVM targets are compiled through invokedynamic/LambdaMetafactory by default. -Xsam-conversions=class restores the older generated-class approach. On Android, D8/R8 desugars that invokedynamic back into synthetic classes, so at runtime you still get small classes. The compilation of plain Kotlin lambdas (and the Kotlin 2.0 switch to indy for them) belongs to K3a.
lambda { it % 2 == 0 }
   |
   +-- expected (Int) -> Boolean  --> Function1 instance (boxes Int)
   |
   +-- expected IntPredicate      --> IntPredicate instance, accept(int) primitive
       (fun interface / Java SAM)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface PlainValidator { fun validate(s: String): Boolean }
fun interface Validator { fun validate(s: String): Boolean
    fun and(other: Validator): Validator = Validator { validate(it) && other.validate(it) } // non-abstract ok
}

fun register(v: Validator) {}
fun registerPlain(v: PlainValidator) {}

fun demo() {
    register { it.isNotBlank() }                     // OK: fun interface
    val v = Validator { it.length > 3 }              // SAM constructor syntax
    // registerPlain { it.isNotBlank() }             // compile error: not a fun interface
    registerPlain(object : PlainValidator {          // must use an object expression
        override fun validate(s: String) = s.isNotBlank()
    })
    java.util.concurrent.Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor().execute { println("Java SAM, always works") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking SAM conversion "doesn't work for Kotlin interfaces at all". That has been wrong since 1.4. You just need fun.
  • Adding a second abstract method to a published fun interface. That is a compile error in the declaration and breaks every lambda call site downstream.
  • Assuming a lambda converted to an interface has stable identity. It does not (see Q102).
  • Declaring fun interface with an abstract val. It fails to compile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a fun interface be generic? → Yes, e.g. fun interface Mapper<in T, out R> { fun map(t: T): R }.
  2. Can I use a callable reference instead of a lambda? → Yes, register(::isEmail). The docs call this SAM adaptation. Callable references to a functional interface's constructor (::Validator) are supported since Kotlin 1.6.20.
  3. Why would I pick a fun interface over (String) -> Boolean in a public API? → Java callers get a void/primitive-friendly method, I get a named type for extensions and docs, primitives avoid boxing, and I can add default methods later. Q105 covers this in depth.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer stops at "lambdas work for Java interfaces, use fun interface for Kotlin ones". The senior adds why the conversion is opt-in (it freezes the contract), what it compiles to (indy since 1.5, desugared by D8 on Android), the primitive-boxing difference versus function types, and the identity caveat for listener removal.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared UI library converted interface OnItemClick to fun interface to tidy call sites. That was fine. A later PR added a second abstract method "for long press", and 140 lambda call sites across 12 modules stopped compiling. The safe move was a separate interface or a default method.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the kinds of callable references in Kotlin (::foo, Type::member, ::Constructor, property references). What type does each have?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: References appear all over Android code (map(::toUi), setOnClickListener(viewModel::onClick)). The interviewer wants to know you understand their types, overload resolution, and that calling them does not need reflection.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A callable reference turns a named function, constructor or property into a function value without writing a lambda. ::topLevel has type (A) -> R. String::length is an unbound member reference: the receiver becomes the first parameter, so its type is (String) -> Int. ::User references a constructor and has type (String, Int) -> User. User::name is a KProperty1<User, String>, which is also usable as (User) -> String. All of them implement KFunction/KProperty, but invoking them is a plain call. Only introspection, such as reading parameters or annotations, needs kotlin-reflect.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reference Example Function type it fits Reflection type
Top-level / local function ::parse (String) -> Int KFunction1<String, Int>
Unbound member String::trim (String) -> String KFunction1<String, String>
Unbound extension String::isEmail (String) -> Boolean KFunction1
Constructor ::User (String, Int) -> User KFunction2
Unbound property User::name (User) -> String KProperty1<User, String>
Bound member/property user::name, vm::load () -> String, (Id) -> Unit KProperty0, KFunction1 (Q098)
  • Overload resolution. ::parse is ambiguous when overloads exist. The compiler picks the overload from the expected type: val f: (String) -> Int = ::parse. Without an expected type you get "overload resolution ambiguity".
  • Adapted references (Kotlin 1.4+). A reference can match a function type even when the target has default parameters (they are filled in), a vararg (it can be fed by a fixed number of arguments), or returns a value where Unit is expected (the value is coerced away). A non-suspend function reference is also accepted where a suspend function type is expected.
  • Compilation. On the JVM a reference becomes a synthetic class or an indy-generated object that implements FunctionN and extends FunctionReference/PropertyReference. Those base classes carry metadata (name, owner, signature) so toString() and equals work without kotlin-reflect. Calling .parameters, .annotations or callBy does need the kotlin-reflect artifact (about 3 MB before shrinking; reflection cost is covered in K11).
  • Passed to an inline function, e.g. list.map(::toUi), the reference is inlined like a lambda and no object is allocated.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)
fun parse(s: String): Int = s.toInt()
fun parse(s: String, radix: Int): Int = s.toInt(radix)
fun String.isEmail() = contains('@')
fun log(msg: String, tag: String = "App") = println("$tag: $msg")

fun demo(rows: List<String>) {
    val f: (String) -> Int = ::parse                // expected type selects overload
    val ages = rows.map(::parse)                    // also resolved by map's expected type
    val emails = rows.filter(String::isEmail)
    val make: (String, Int) -> User = ::User
    val nameOf: (User) -> String = User::name
    val logger: (String) -> Unit = ::log            // adapted: default `tag` filled in (1.4+)
    // val g = ::parse                              // error: ambiguity, no expected type
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming ::foo uses reflection and is slow. Invocation is a normal virtual call.
  • Using User::name with Gson/Moshi-style "property name" logic and then hitting an R8 rename. KProperty.name comes from Kotlin metadata, which stays correct, but string keys built for a reflective serializer may not match the obfuscated field.
  • Forgetting the expected type when the target is overloaded.
  • Confusing String::length (one parameter) with "abc"::length (zero parameters).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you reference a generic function? → Yes, but the type arguments must be inferable from the expected type, e.g. val f: (List<Int>) -> Int = List<Int>::size or ::listOf with an expected type.
  2. Is ::User usable from Java? → Not as a lambda. Java sees a Kotlin object implementing Function2. In Java, use User::new.
  3. Does list.map(::toUi) allocate? → No. map is inline, so the reference is inlined. For a non-inline higher-order function it allocates a reference object, or reuses a singleton when nothing is captured.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev knows :: passes a function. The senior lists the reference kinds with their arity, explains expected-type overload resolution, adapted references, and the metadata-versus-kotlin-reflect boundary, and knows inline call sites are allocation-free.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team pulled in kotlin-reflect "because we use :: everywhere". The app grew by roughly 2 MB pre-R8 with zero benefit, since no code ever called reflection APIs on those references.

questions.promptHtml: How do default and named arguments work, and what does the compiler actually generate for a function with default parameters?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most devs use defaults daily. Few know about the $default synthetic, the bitmask, or how overrides inherit defaults. That knowledge underpins @JvmOverloads, Java interop and ABI questions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A default argument is an expression evaluated at the call site only when the caller omits that argument. The compiler emits the real method with all parameters, plus a static synthetic method foo$default that takes the same parameters, an int bitmask saying which ones were omitted, and a marker object. The caller passes placeholder values (zeros or nulls) and the mask. The $default method fills in the defaults and calls the real method. Named arguments are purely a compile-time feature: the compiler reorders them into positional order. Java sees only the full-arity method, which is why @JvmOverloads exists.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Evaluation. Default expressions run on every call where the argument is omitted, in parameter order. They can reference earlier parameters (fun pad(s: String, width: Int = s.length + 2)) and members of the receiver. A call like now() as a default runs per call, not once.
  • Generated code (JVM):
fun load(id: String, page: Int = 0, force: Boolean = false)

=> public final void load(String id, int page, boolean force)
=> public static void load$default(Owner self, String id, int page, boolean force,
                                   int mask, Object marker)
     if (mask & 0b010) page  = 0
     if (mask & 0b100) force = false
     self.load(id, page, force)

call site load("42", force = true)  ->  load$default(this, "42", 0, true, 0b010, null)
  • There is one mask bit per parameter, and one extra int mask for every 32 parameters.
  • The marker Object parameter keeps the synthetic signature from clashing with a user-written overload.
  • The synthetic method is static and takes the receiver explicitly. That is how overrides "inherit" defaults: the call dispatches virtually to the real method after the defaults are applied.
  • Overrides. An overriding function cannot redeclare default values (compile error). It always uses the base declaration's defaults. Interface functions can declare defaults too.
  • Named arguments:
    • The compiler maps names to positions.
    • Since Kotlin 1.4 you can mix named and positional arguments as long as every positional argument is in its correct position.
    • You cannot use named arguments when calling Java methods, because parameter names are not reliably present in Java bytecode.
    • Argument expressions are evaluated in the order written at the call site, not in declaration order.
  • Trailing lambda + defaults. A function type in the last position can follow omitted defaults: retry(times = 3) { ... }.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Repo {
    fun load(id: String, page: Int = 0, force: Boolean = false, at: Long = System.currentTimeMillis()) {}
}
open class Base { open fun greet(name: String = "you") = "hi $name" }
class Child : Base() {
    override fun greet(name: String) = "hey $name"   // cannot write `= "x"` here; Base default applies
}

fun demo(repo: Repo) {
    repo.load("42", force = true)        // page=0, at evaluated now
    repo.load(id = "42", 2, true)        // 1.4+: positional after named is ok in correct position
    println(Child().greet())             // "hey you": default from Base, body from Child
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking a default like System.currentTimeMillis() or UUID.randomUUID() is computed once. It runs per call.
  • Expecting Java to see the defaults. Java must pass every argument unless @JvmOverloads is used.
  • Adding a defaulted parameter and assuming it is binary compatible. Both the real method and the $default signature change (Q110).
  • Using defaults on an open function and expecting subclasses to change them.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Are default values part of the ABI? → Not the values: they live inside the $default body in the declaring module, so changing a value takes effect without recompiling callers. The parameter list is part of the ABI.
  2. What about inline functions with defaults? → The defaults are inlined at the call site along with the body, so changing them needs callers to recompile.
  3. Can a default reference a later parameter? → No. Only earlier parameters and the scope are visible.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "defaults replace overloads, named args improve readability". The senior describes $default with the bitmask and marker, per-call evaluation, override inheritance, the Java-visibility gap, and which changes are binary-safe versus source-safe.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A createdAt: Long = System.currentTimeMillis() default in a data model was assumed to be "row creation time". Copies made with copy() kept the original value, while new objects built via a secondary path got a fresh one. The sync engine then mis-ordered edits. Time belongs in an injected Clock, not a default.

questions.promptHtml: How does vararg work in Kotlin, what is the spread operator, and what does it cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It looks trivial, but it exposes understanding of array types (IntArray vs Array<out T>), hidden copies on hot paths, and Java varargs interop.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A vararg parameter collects zero or more arguments into an array. For primitives it is a primitive array, so vararg xs: Int is an IntArray. Otherwise it is Array<out T>. If I already have an array, I pass it with the spread operator *arr. Spreading copies the array, so the callee can never mutate mine. Combining *a, x, *b builds a new array. There can be only one vararg per function. If it isn't last, the parameters after it must be named or be a trailing lambda.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Types:
Declaration Type inside the function JVM signature
vararg xs: Int IntArray int...
vararg xs: String Array<out String> String...
vararg xs: Int? Array<out Int?> Integer... (boxed)
  • Spread semantics. foo(*arr) passes a copy (Arrays.copyOf) to a Kotlin vararg. foo(*a, 1, *b) uses a spread builder to concatenate into a new array. There is no "pass by reference" mode for Kotlin varargs.
  • Collections. A List cannot be spread directly. You write *list.toTypedArray(), which costs one copy for toTypedArray plus one copy for the spread. On a 10k-element list that is two 10k-element array copies per call.
  • Java interop. Calling a Java String... method: pass items or *array. A Java method declared with varargs is seen from Kotlin as vararg, so calling String.format(fmt, *args) is the idiom. A Kotlin vararg is visible to Java as a normal varargs method.
  • Named vararg. You can pass an array to a vararg by name with spread: format(args = *arr).
  • Hot-path cost. Every call allocates an array, even for one argument. listOf(a, b, c) allocates a 3-element array plus the list wrapper. In a RecyclerView bind or a draw loop this is measurable garbage. A fixed-arity overload avoids it, which is why the stdlib has listOf(element) and setOf(element) single-argument overloads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun sum(vararg xs: Int): Int = xs.sum()          // xs: IntArray
fun tags(prefix: String, vararg names: String, sep: String = ",") =
    names.joinToString(sep) { "$prefix$it" }

fun demo(ids: IntArray, list: List<String>) {
    sum()                          // empty IntArray
    sum(1, 2, 3)
    sum(*ids)                      // copies ids
    sum(0, *ids, 99)               // builds a new array of ids.size + 2
    tags("#", *list.toTypedArray(), sep = "|")   // two copies; `sep` must be named after vararg
    String.format("%s=%d", *arrayOf<Any>("n", 1))
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing an array without *. sum(ids) is a type error, while a vararg xs: Any would silently receive the array as a single element.
  • Relying on the callee to fill or mutate the caller's array. It only mutates the copy.
  • Using vararg in per-frame or per-bind code without noticing the allocation.
  • Declaring a vararg in the middle and forgetting that subsequent args must be named.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. fun log(vararg args: Any) called with log(arrayOf(1, 2)): what does the function see? → One element, which is the array itself. You need log(*arrayOf(1, 2)).
  2. Can a function reference target a vararg function? → Yes. Since 1.4 adapted references can match (Int, Int) -> Int to sum.
  3. How do you avoid the copy entirely? → Take an IntArray/List parameter explicitly instead of a vararg. That is a deliberate API choice when callers already hold arrays.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The junior says "vararg = many args, * spreads an array". The senior gives the primitive-array mapping, the copy-on-spread guarantee and its cost (with the double copy via toTypedArray), the Any vararg pitfall, and when to replace varargs with explicit array or list parameters.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A logging helper fun d(vararg parts: Any?) was called inside onDraw of a custom chart, at 60 fps with roughly 40 calls per frame. That is 2,400 array allocations per second (60 × 40), which showed up as GC churn in the Memory Profiler. Gating the call behind if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) plus a fixed-arity overload removed the churn.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between viewModel::onClick and { viewModel.onClick() }? When is the receiver evaluated, and why does it matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Bound references evaluate their receiver eagerly. That causes real bugs with lateinit, swapped dependencies and leaks, and it separates people who "use the syntax" from people who know the semantics.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bound reference expr::member evaluates expr once, when the reference is created, and stores that object inside the function value. A lambda { expr.member() } captures the enclosing scope and re-evaluates expr every time it is invoked. So if the receiver is a lateinit not yet initialized, the reference throws immediately. If the receiver is later replaced, the reference still points at the old object. The reference also holds a strong reference to that receiver for as long as the function value lives.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
val r = presenter::onClick
  -> evaluate `presenter` now -> P1
  -> object { val receiver = P1; fun invoke() = receiver.onClick() }

val l = { presenter.onClick() }
  -> object { val outer = this@Screen; fun invoke() = outer.presenter.onClick() }
                                       ^ read at call time
  • Typing. String::length is unbound, (String) -> Int. "abc"::length is bound, () -> Int. this::onEvent is bound to this. Inside a class you can write ::onEvent, and it resolves to the bound this::onEvent.
  • Eager evaluation consequences:
    1. A lateinit var presenter accessed through presenter::onClick in onCreate, before injection, throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException at registration time, not at click time.
    2. If the dependency is swapped, for example a scoped object recreated after logout, the old instance keeps receiving calls.
    3. A null-safe receiver is not allowed: maybe?::foo does not compile. You need maybe?.let { it::foo }.
  • Retention. A bound reference keeps exactly the receiver alive. A lambda keeps alive whatever it captures, often this (an Activity or Fragment) if it touches any member. Neither is automatically leak-safe. It depends on who holds the function value (Q107).
  • Equality. Kotlin reference objects implement equals based on receiver plus callable signature, so in Kotlin a::foo == a::foo is generally true even though they are different instances. Do not build listener removal on that. After SAM conversion to a Java interface the wrapper's equality is identity-based in practice and not specified (Q102).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ScreenController(private val button: android.view.View) {
    lateinit var presenter: Presenter

    fun bindTooEarly() {
        button.setOnClickListener { presenter.onClick() }   // fine: read at click time
        // button.setOnClickListener(presenter::onClick)    // crashes NOW if not injected yet
    }

    fun onSessionChanged(newPresenter: Presenter) {
        presenter = newPresenter
        // listeners built from `presenter::onClick` earlier still call the OLD presenter
    }
}
interface Presenter { fun onClick(v: android.view.View? = null) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating x::f and { x.f() } as identical "style choices".
  • Using bound references to a scoped object inside a long-lived holder (a singleton event bus, an app-scoped Flow) and leaking that scope.
  • Assuming a bound reference avoids capturing an Activity. If the receiver is the Activity (this::render), it captures it.
  • Expecting obj?::method to compile.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is this::render cheaper than { render(it) }? → Comparable. Both allocate one small object at a non-inline site. With an inline target, both inline. Choose on semantics, not cost.
  2. How does a bound reference behave with by lazy receivers? → The lazy property is read when the reference is created, so it forces initialization at that point.
  3. Can you get the receiver back from a bound reference? → Through kotlin-reflect, KFunction has boundReceiver on CallableReference (an internal-ish JVM API). Don't design around it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev says they are equivalent. The senior explains eager receiver evaluation, the lateinit crash timing, stale receivers after dependency swaps, what each form retains for GC, and why reference equality is not a removal strategy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a "log out and switch account" feature shipped, analytics events went to the previous user's tracker. A screen registered tracker::log once at startup, and the tracker was recreated per account. Switching to { trackerProvider().log(it) } fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: How does SAM interop work in both directions: Kotlin calling Java SAM APIs, and Java calling Kotlin APIs that take function types?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most Android codebases are mixed. The return Unit.INSTANCE pain, SAM constructors and overload ambiguity are everyday interop issues for a senior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin calling Java is easy. Any Java interface with one abstract method accepts a Kotlin lambda, and I can use a SAM constructor such as Runnable { } when the compiler needs the type spelled out, for example for a variable or to break overload ambiguity. Java calling Kotlin is the awkward direction. A Kotlin (String) -> Unit parameter appears in Java as Function1<? super String, Unit>, so a Java lambda must return Unit.INSTANCE;. If an API will be called from Java, I expose a fun interface with a void-returning method instead of a function type.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Kotlin → Java:
    • Lambdas convert to any Java SAM: view.setOnClickListener { }, executor.execute { }.
    • Parameters arrive as platform types (View!), so null-safety is on you.
    • A SAM constructor OnClickListener { v -> ... } creates an instance explicitly. It is required when there is no expected interface type, like val l = Runnable { }, or when overloads accept different SAMs and the lambda shape fits more than one. A classic example is ExecutorService.submit(Runnable) vs submit(Callable<T>): write submit(Callable { compute() }) to be explicit.
    • Since Kotlin 1.4, Kotlin functions that take Java SAM types also accept lambdas.
  • Java → Kotlin function types:
Kotlin:  fun fetch(onDone: (String) -> Unit)
Java  :  void fetch(Function1<? super String, Unit> onDone)
Java call: repo.fetch(s -> { show(s); return Unit.INSTANCE; });
  • Primitive parameters box: a Kotlin (Int) -> Boolean is Function1<Integer, Boolean>.
  • More than 22 parameters maps to FunctionN, which Java can't use nicely.
  • Suspend function types expose an extra Continuation parameter that Java essentially can't satisfy (see C1b for calling suspend from Java).
  • Java → Kotlin fun interface: fun interface Callback { fun onDone(s: String) } is a normal Java interface with a void method, so a Java lambda s -> show(s) just works.
  • Default methods in Java SAMs: they are fine. Only abstract methods count, and methods matching Object members are ignored.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Library API designed for both languages
fun interface ResultCallback { fun onResult(value: String) }

class Repo {
    fun fetchKotlinStyle(onDone: (String) -> Unit) = onDone("k")    // Java: return Unit.INSTANCE
    fun fetch(cb: ResultCallback) = cb.onResult("j")                 // Java: s -> show(s)
}

fun kotlinSide(executor: java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService) {
    val r = Runnable { println("needs SAM constructor: no expected type") }
    executor.execute(r)
    val f = executor.submit(java.util.concurrent.Callable { 42 })    // explicit, picks Callable
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Shipping Kotlin function types in an SDK whose customers are largely Java. Every call site gets return Unit.INSTANCE noise.
  • Trusting nullability of SAM parameters coming from Java (v: View!). Some framework callbacks really do pass null.
  • Overload ambiguity after a library adds a second SAM overload. Previously compiling lambdas become ambiguous.
  • Assuming a function type is cheaper than a fun interface for primitives. It boxes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does SAM conversion work for a Java abstract class with one abstract method? → No, only interfaces. Use an object : expression.
  2. Why can't Java use Kotlin named/default args on a callback API? → Java has neither feature. Provide overloads (@JvmOverloads, Q103) or a builder.
  3. How do you keep both nice? → A fun interface for Java plus Kotlin-only inline extension helpers taking lambdas. Since the SAM conversion is automatic, Kotlin callers lose nothing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev knows lambdas work with Java listeners. The senior also covers the reverse direction (Function1, Unit.INSTANCE, boxing), SAM constructors for ambiguity, and frames API choice around the actual caller population.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An internal payments SDK exposed (PaymentResult) -> Unit. The Java-based merchant app wrapped it in 30 adapters to hide Unit.INSTANCE. Version 2 switched to fun interface PaymentListener, with a deprecated overload kept for one release.

questions.promptHtml: What is a function type with receiver like StringBuilder.() -> Unit, how does it differ from (StringBuilder) -> Unit, and how does it compile?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the mechanism behind apply, buildString, Compose scopes and every DSL. Understanding it as a type, rather than as magic, is the signal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A.() -> R is a function type whose first parameter is an implicit receiver. Inside the lambda, this is the A, so I can call its members unqualified. On the JVM it is exactly the same as (A) -> R: a Function1<A, R> where the receiver is just the first argument. The difference is only in the lambda body's scope and in how you call it: sb.block() or block(sb). Non-literal values of the two types are even assignable to each other.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Type-level: A.(B) -> C means "receiver A, parameter B, returns C". Calling a value f of this type: a.f(b) or f(a, b), both are legal.
  • In the lambda literal: this refers to the receiver. Unqualified member calls resolve against it first, then against outer scopes. this@outer reaches enclosing receivers.
  • Interchangeability: the docs state that non-literal values of function types with and without a receiver are interchangeable, so a (StringBuilder) -> Unit value can be passed where StringBuilder.() -> Unit is expected and vice versa. A lambda literal gets its scope from the expected type: with a receiver type you get this, without one you get it.
  • Compilation: a Function1<A, R> whose invoke(a) binds a as this in the body. Passed to an inline function such as apply or buildString, the body is inlined and the receiver is just a local.
  • Why it exists: it lets an API configure an object or expose a scope (buildList { add(1) }, CoroutineScope.() -> Unit in launch) while the caller writes code that reads like it's inside the object. Builder DSLs and @DslMarker are covered in K9. Choosing between apply and also is covered in K4.
StringBuilder.() -> Unit   ==JVM==   Function1<StringBuilder, Unit>
       |                                   |
 body sees `this: StringBuilder`     invoke(sb) passes sb as arg 0

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
inline fun html(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString()

fun demo() {
    val s = html { append("<b>"); append("hi"); append("</b>") }    // `this` is StringBuilder

    val withReceiver: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = { append("x") }
    val plain: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = withReceiver               // assignable
    val back: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = plain                      // and back
    val sb = StringBuilder()
    sb.withReceiver()          // receiver-style call
    withReceiver(sb)           // plain call, same thing
    plain(sb)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Name shadowing: inside A.() -> Unit, an unqualified name may resolve to A.name instead of your outer property (the apply shadowing scenario is in K4).
  • Believing receiver lambdas are slower or "reflective". They are identical to plain Function1.
  • Using a receiver type in an API where the receiver isn't conceptually "the scope". (Item) -> Unit is clearer for callbacks.
  • Forgetting this@Outer when both the outer class and the receiver have a member with the same name.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does launch take suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit? → So the body can call launch/async and read coroutineContext on the child's own scope without qualification. That is the basis of structured concurrency syntax (C4).
  2. Can an extension function be passed where A.() -> R is expected? → Yes, via reference: String::shout fits String.() -> String.
  3. What is the difference from context parameters? → A receiver is one implicit this. Context parameters (preview in Kotlin 2.2; see K11 for status) let you require several implicit values without making them this.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev says "it lets you use this inside the lambda". The senior adds JVM equivalence with Function1, call-syntax duality, value interchangeability, resolution and shadowing order, and when a receiver type is the wrong API shape.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A theming helper took Paint.() -> Unit. Inside, an unqualified color = accent resolved to Paint.color, which was intended. A later refactor added a color property to the enclosing class, and readers misread which one was set. A code review rule now asks for explicit this. in receiver lambdas that mutate.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use a local function instead of a private function or a lambda, and what do local functions compile to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes code-organization judgment and closure-capture understanding, which is how a local function can quietly capture mutable state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A local function is a fun declared inside another function. It can read and write the enclosing function's locals and parameters, so I use it for a helper that only makes sense inside one function, like validation steps that share the same inputs, without widening the class API or passing six parameters around. Unlike a lambda it can be recursive, have default arguments and be generic, and a plain call allocates nothing. With the current JVM IR backend it is lifted to a private static method on the enclosing class, with captured values passed as extra parameters and captured vars wrapped in Ref objects.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Capabilities vs lambda:
Local fun Lambda in a val
Recursion yes awkward (needs lateinit var or DeepRecursiveFunction)
Default/named args, generics yes no generics, no defaults
return returns from itself return@label only, or non-local if inlined
Allocation on call none function object allocated (unless no capture → may be cached)
Pass as value ::local creates a function object already a value
  • Compilation (verify with "Show Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile"):
    • The JVM IR backend (default since Kotlin 1.5) emits something like private static final boolean validate$isValidEmail(String captured, String s).
    • Captured vals become parameters.
    • A captured var that the local function mutates is boxed into Ref.IntRef/Ref.ObjectRef so both scopes see the same cell. That is the same mechanism as lambda var capture covered in K3a.
    • Older backends generated a Function object for the local function. Don't quote that as current behaviour.
  • Restrictions:
    • Local functions cannot be inline (not supported).
    • They can't have visibility modifiers.
    • They are not visible to tests, which can be a pro or a con.
  • When not to use:
    • If the outer function grows past roughly 50 lines because of nested helpers, extract a class or private functions.
    • Deep nesting of local functions that mutate shared captured vars reads like hidden global state.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun validate(form: SignupForm): List<String> {
    val errors = mutableListOf<String>()
    var checks = 0                                      // captured var -> Ref.IntRef

    fun require(ok: Boolean, msg: String) {             // captures errors + checks
        checks++
        if (!ok) errors += msg
    }
    fun isStrong(p: String, minLen: Int = 8): Boolean =  // default arg: lambdas can't do this
        p.length >= minLen && p.any(Char::isDigit)

    require(form.email.contains('@'), "email")
    require(isStrong(form.password), "password")
    require(form.password == form.confirm, "confirm")
    return errors
}

fun countNodes(root: Node?): Int {
    fun go(n: Node?): Int = if (n == null) 0 else 1 + go(n.left) + go(n.right)   // recursion ok
    return go(root)
}
data class SignupForm(val email: String, val password: String, val confirm: String)
class Node(val left: Node?, val right: Node?)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming captured var mutation is thread-safe. The Ref cell is a plain field. If the local function is passed (::require) into a concurrent context, you have a race.
  • Using a local function where a top-level private function would be reusable and testable.
  • Expecting ::local to be free. Taking a reference creates a function object.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a local function be a suspend fun? → Yes, inside a suspend function. It participates in the CPS transform like any suspend function.
  2. Can you declare a local class or object? → Yes. Local classes capture the same way.
  3. How would you test a local function's logic? → You don't directly. If it's complex enough to need tests, it shouldn't be local.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev says "a function inside a function for readability". The senior compares it against lambdas (recursion, defaults, generics, zero allocation), explains the static-method lifting and Ref boxing, and states the threshold where it should become a class.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A local fun emit() captured a var count and was passed into a parallelStream().forEach. Totals came out wrong on 8-core devices. The Ref.IntRef was shared across threads with no synchronization.

questions.contextHtml:
A video player screen integrates a Java SDK. After QA navigates in and out of the player 10 times, CPU usage on a Pixel 6a sits at 35% while idle, render() logs fire 10 times per state change, and LeakCanary reports 9 retained PlayerScreen instances. Crash-free rate is unaffected. Someone points at the new ExoPlayer version upgraded in the same release (red herring). Code:

// Java SDK: public interface StateListener { void onState(int state); }
//           void addStateListener(StateListener l); void removeStateListener(StateListener l);

class PlayerScreen(private val sdk: VideoSdk) {
    fun onStart() {
        sdk.addStateListener { state -> render(state) }
    }
    fun onStop() {
        sdk.removeStateListener { state -> render(state) }   // "same lambda"
    }
    private fun render(state: Int) { /* updates views */ }
}

A teammate's "fix" changes both lines to sdk.addStateListener(::render) / sdk.removeStateListener(::render).
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, why doesn't the teammate's fix work, and what's the correct fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The lambdas are the same code, so remove should work. Maybe the SDK has a bug, or the ExoPlayer upgrade changed behaviour." Or accepting ::render because "references are equal in Kotlin". Both miss that each SAM conversion creates a new interface instance, and the SDK compares with equals/identity on that instance.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does the SDK store listeners in a List/Set compared by equals? That decides whether any equality trick could ever work.
    • Is the player screen a Fragment or Activity, and are onStart/onStop paired? That rules out lifecycle mismatch.
    • Did listener count grow before the ExoPlayer upgrade? That isolates the red herring.
  2. Immediate mitigation: This is a resource and leak bug, not a crash. Hot-fix by holding the listener in a field, and ship it in the next build. If the SDK exposes clearListeners(), call it in onStop as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Each { state -> render(state) } passed to a Java SAM parameter is converted to a new StateListener object. The remove call passes an object the SDK has never seen, so it is a no-op.
    2. The lambda captures this, because render is a member, so every un-removed listener retains a PlayerScreen. That matches the 9 retained instances.
    3. The ExoPlayer upgrade: unlikely, since the symptom scales exactly with navigation count.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Log System.identityHashCode(listener) at add and remove. The values differ.
    • Use a debugger on the SDK's listener list size.
    • LeakCanary's trace: VideoSdk.listeners → ArrayList → PlayerScreen$onStart$1 (or $$Lambda) → this$0 PlayerScreen.
    • Revert ExoPlayer locally: the symptom persists.
  5. Root cause: SAM conversion produces an interface instance per evaluation of the lambda expression when it captures anything (here it captures this). Since Kotlin 1.5 it is built via invokedynamic, which D8 desugars to a synthetic class on Android, and the result has identity-based equals. The teammate's ::render fix fails for the same reason. A bound reference converted to a Java SAM is also a fresh wrapper per evaluation, and its equals is not something the language guarantees. Even where Kotlin's own function-reference objects compare structurally, the SAM wrapper the SDK receives is a different object.
  6. Fix:
class PlayerScreen(private val sdk: VideoSdk) {
    private val listener = StateListener { state -> render(state) }   // one instance, stored

    fun onStart() = sdk.addStateListener(listener)
    fun onStop()  = sdk.removeStateListener(listener)
    private fun render(state: Int) { /* ... */ }
}

Longer term, wrap the SDK in a callbackFlow repository (see C10) and collect it with repeatOnLifecycle, so registration and unregistration are structurally paired. 7. Prevention:

  • Review rule: "every removeXListener must receive a stored instance".
  • A custom lint or detekt check flagging a lambda or ::ref argument to methods named remove*Listener/unregister*.
  • LeakCanary in debug builds and an instrumentation test that navigates 5× and asserts the SDK listener count.
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't rely on "non-capturing lambdas are singletons". It's an implementation detail of indy/desugaring and breaks the moment the lambda touches a member.
    • I wouldn't override equals on some wrapper to make lambdas "equal". That is fragile and surprising.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the SDK is Kotlin and takes (Int) -> Unit? → Same bug. A new lambda object per evaluation, and identity comparison by default. Store it in a val.
  • What if the listener must be different per registration, for example to track which one fired? → Use object : StateListener {} or a class. The fun interface docs explicitly warn that SAM conversion may not preserve distinct identity semantics.
  • Does view.setOnClickListener {} have this problem? → No. It replaces a single slot, so there is no removal by identity. Multi-listener APIs (addTextChangedListener, addOnScrollListener) do.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sensor dashboard leaked one SensorEventListener per resume because unregister was called with a fresh lambda. Battery drain complaints rose before anyone looked at the code. A field-stored listener fixed it in one line, and the lint check stopped the next three occurrences.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: thinks identical lambda bodies are the same object, or blames the SDK or ExoPlayer.
  • Hire: identifies new-instance-per-conversion, stores the listener in a field, explains the this capture leak.
  • Strong hire: also explains why ::render fails, uses identity-hash logging and LeakCanary to verify, proposes a callbackFlow wrapper and lint prevention, and mentions the doc caveat on identity.

questions.contextHtml:
A team migrates its design-system module from Java to Kotlin, 40 custom views, using the IDE converter plus cleanup. One of them:

class PrimaryChip @JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context,
    attrs: AttributeSet? = null,
    defStyleAttr: Int = 0
) : com.google.android.material.button.MaterialButton(context, attrs, defStyleAttr)

The Java original had three constructors, and the 2-arg one called super(context, attrs). After a 10% staged rollout (about 120k DAU), screenshot tests are green (they use programmatic construction with an explicit style), but users report chips "look like plain text": no background tint, no ripple, wrong padding, on every inflated chip. A dark-mode theme change in the same release is suspected (red herring).
questions.promptHtml: What happened, how do you confirm it, and how should the constructor be written?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Theme regression from the dark-mode change, revert the theme." Or "@JvmOverloads is the standard way to write custom views." That idiom is exactly what broke here, and the answer misses that 0 is not the same as "use the default style".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Are only XML-inflated chips affected, or programmatic ones too? Inflation uses the 2-arg constructor.
    • Which views were converted in this release?
    • Did the Java version pass a non-zero defStyleAttr anywhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the rollout at 10%. The visual regression is user-facing but not a crash, so I'd hotfix rather than roll back the whole release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. @JvmOverloads generates PrimaryChip(Context, AttributeSet?) as this(context, attrs, 0), so MaterialButton receives defStyleAttr = 0 instead of its own default R.attr.materialButtonStyle. Theme-provided styling is skipped.
    2. Dark-mode theme change: would affect programmatic and inflated chips alike, and would affect other components too.
    3. A Material library version bump: check the dependency diff.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Decompile the Kotlin class: the 2-arg constructor calls the 3-arg one with 0.
    • Layout Inspector on an affected screen: the chip's background tint is null and textAppearance is the default.
    • Toggle dark mode off: still broken, so the theme is ruled out.
    • A unit test using Robolectric inflating the XML and asserting backgroundTintList != null.
  5. Root cause: @JvmOverloads on a constructor creates overloads that drop trailing defaulted parameters and fill in the Kotlin default. Here the Kotlin default 0 means "no default style attribute". The platform's 2-arg View(Context, AttributeSet) constructor for Material/AppCompat widgets instead passes the widget's own style attribute (for MaterialButton, R.attr.materialButtonStyle). The Java code relied on super(context, attrs) to do that, and the conversion replaced it with an explicit 0.
  6. Fix:
// Option A: explicit constructors that delegate to the matching super, exactly like the Java original
class PrimaryChip : MaterialButton {
    constructor(context: Context) : super(context)
    constructor(context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet?) : super(context, attrs)
    constructor(context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet?, defStyleAttr: Int) : super(context, attrs, defStyleAttr)
}

// Option B: keep @JvmOverloads but default to the parent's style attr
class PrimaryChip2 @JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context,
    attrs: AttributeSet? = null,
    defStyleAttr: Int = com.google.android.material.R.attr.materialButtonStyle
) : MaterialButton(context, attrs, defStyleAttr)

I prefer Option A for widgets you subclass, because it doesn't hard-code knowledge of the parent's internal default. @JvmOverloads constructor(..., defStyleAttr = 0) is fine when extending a plain View/FrameLayout whose own default is 0. 7. Prevention:

  • Audit all 40 converted views with a grep for @JvmOverloads constructor on classes extending Material/AppCompat widgets.
  • Screenshot tests that inflate from XML, not just programmatic construction.
  • A detekt/lint rule flagging defStyleAttr: Int = 0 when the superclass is not View/ViewGroup.
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't revert the whole Kotlin migration. The bug is one idiom.
    • I wouldn't patch it per-screen with style= in XML. That hides the bug and diverges from the theme.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What does @JvmOverloads generate in general? → For N trailing defaulted parameters, N extra overloads, each dropping the last default. It can't produce "skip the middle one" combinations. It applies to functions and constructors, but the compiler rejects it on interface and abstract methods (K11 covers the full annotation set).
  • Do Kotlin callers use the generated overloads? → No. Kotlin calls go through $default. The overloads exist for Java and for reflection-driven callers like LayoutInflater, which looks up the (Context, AttributeSet) constructor reflectively.
  • What if you omit @JvmOverloads entirely? → Inflation crashes with NoSuchMethodException for the 2-arg constructor, wrapped as an InflateException.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A converted AppCompatEditText subclass lost its tint and underline only on API 21–23 devices, where the theme fallback differed. It took a week because the screenshot suite used API 33 emulators. The fix was explicit constructors plus an API 23 screenshot target.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the theme, or doesn't know what @JvmOverloads generates.
  • Hire: explains the 0 vs parent default-style attr issue and writes correct constructors.
  • Strong hire: also covers why inflation needs the 2-arg constructor (reflection), when @JvmOverloads is safe, a grep/lint audit, and inflating screenshot tests.

questions.promptHtml: What does operator fun invoke give you, where is it a good idea (use cases, function-like classes, factory-style companions), and where does it hurt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Clean-architecture "UseCase with invoke" is everywhere in Android codebases. Interviewers want to see that you know the mechanism and can judge readability and testability trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Declaring operator fun invoke(...) lets an instance be called like a function: getUser(id) instead of getUser.execute(id). It's what function types use under the hood, since a lambda's f(x) is f.invoke(x). Good uses are single-responsibility use cases, classes that implement a function type like (Event) -> Unit, and a companion invoke as a pseudo-constructor that validates or returns a different implementation. It hurts when it hides that an object is being called, when there are several overloaded invokes, or when nullable function properties need ?.invoke().

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Resolution. x(args) resolves to a member or extension invoke on x's type. For a property of function type, onClick() calls onClick.invoke(). A member function named onClick wins over a property onClick of function type with the same name, which is a classic confusion.
  • Implementing function types. class Formatter : (Long) -> String { override fun invoke(t: Long) = ... }. The instance can be passed anywhere a (Long) -> String is expected, so stateful or injected logic can be passed as a lambda.
  • Companion invoke. companion object { operator fun invoke(raw: String): Email? = ... } makes Email("x") look like a constructor while returning a nullable or a cached instance. This is useful for validation, but it deceives readers: Email("x") returning null surprises people. A named factory like Email.parse() is usually clearer.
  • Use cases:
    • class GetFeed @Inject constructor(...) { suspend operator fun invoke(page: Int): Feed }. suspend operator fun invoke is legal.
    • Call site: val feed = getFeed(1).
    • Mocking: coEvery { getFeed(any()) } works with MockK because it's a normal method named invoke.
  • Nullable function values. val onDone: (() -> Unit)?. You can't write onDone(), you must write onDone?.invoke().
  • Java. It's just a method called invoke. Java callers write getFeed.invoke(1, continuation) for suspend versions, which is ugly but works.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class FormatPrice(private val locale: java.util.Locale) : (Long) -> String {
    override fun invoke(cents: Long): String =
        java.text.NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale).format(cents / 100.0)
}

class GetFeed(private val api: FeedApi) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(page: Int): List<String> = api.feed(page)
}
interface FeedApi { suspend fun feed(page: Int): List<String> }

@JvmInline value class Email private constructor(val value: String) {
    companion object {
        operator fun invoke(raw: String): Email? = raw.takeIf { '@' in it }?.let(::Email)  // surprising nullable "ctor"
    }
}

class Row(val onClick: (() -> Unit)?) {
    fun click() { onClick?.invoke() }          // onClick() won't compile on a nullable type
}

suspend fun demo(getFeed: GetFeed, prices: List<Long>) {
    val feed = getFeed(1)
    val labels = prices.map(FormatPrice(java.util.Locale.US))   // instance used as a function
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Multiple invoke overloads on one use case. Call sites become ambiguous to readers. Split into separate use cases.
  • Companion invoke returning nullable or a different type and being read as a constructor.
  • Forgetting that a member function shadows a function-typed property of the same name.
  • Over-applying "every class gets invoke". Repositories with five methods are not functions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is getFeed(1) slower than getFeed.execute(1)? → No. Identical bytecode, a virtual call to invoke.
  2. Can extension invoke exist? → Yes, operator fun String.invoke(n: Int) = repeat(n). It's technically legal and almost always a bad idea outside DSLs.
  3. How does invoke relate to Compose @Composable lambdas? → Calling content() invokes a function-typed parameter. The Compose compiler rewrites the type to add Composer parameters, but the source-level mechanism is still invoke (K9 covers DSL use).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev knows "use cases use invoke". The senior explains resolution rules (member vs property, nullable ?.invoke()), implementing function types to pass injected logic as lambdas, the deceptive companion-invoke factory, and sets a team convention: one public invoke per use case, with suspend when it does IO.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team's Email(raw) companion invoke returned null for invalid input. A developer assumed it threw, wrote Email(input)!! in a deep link handler, and turned malformed links into crashes. Renaming it to Email.parseOrNull() made the contract visible.

questions.subtopic: fun interface vs function type vs typealias
questions.promptHtml: You're designing a public callback API for a library used by Kotlin and Java apps. Function type, typealias, or fun interface, and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's an API-design question that tests evolution and binary compatibility, Java ergonomics, performance (boxing), and identity, which is staff-level reasoning about a tiny decision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For an internal Kotlin-only callback I use a function type, optionally named with a typealias, because it's the lightest option and any lambda or reference fits. For a public, multi-language or long-lived API I use a fun interface. It gives Java a natural void method and no Unit.INSTANCE, it avoids boxing primitive parameters, it gives me a nominal type I can document and extend, and I can evolve it by adding default methods. A typealias is only a name: zero type safety, and Java sees the raw Function1.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Concern (Int) -> Unit typealias OnProgress = (Int) -> Unit fun interface OnProgress { fun onProgress(p: Int) }
New type? No No (alias erased) Yes
Java signature Function1<Integer, Unit> same void onProgress(int)
Primitive boxing yes (Integer) yes no
Lambda at Kotlin call site yes yes yes (SAM conversion)
Extensions only for this concept no no (applies to all (Int)->Unit) yes
Add a non-abstract method later impossible impossible yes (default method; JVM default-method mode, see K2b)
Distinguish two callbacks of same shape no, mixups compile no yes, different types
Runtime cost lambda object same SAM-converted object, roughly the same
  • Type safety. With function types, fun download(onProgress: (Int) -> Unit, onRetry: (Int) -> Unit) lets a caller swap the two silently. Named fun interfaces make that a compile error.
  • Binary evolution.
    • Changing a function type's arity breaks every caller and implementer.
    • A fun interface can gain default methods. With Kotlin 2.x's default JVM-default behaviour (details in K2b) those are real Java default methods, so Java implementers don't break.
    • It can never gain a second abstract method without breaking lambdas.
  • Performance. (Int) -> Unit boxes on every call. Ints in the Integer cache range (−128..127) avoid allocation. A progress callback firing 0..100 stays in that range, but byte counts don't. A fun interface method takes int directly.
  • Coroutines/Flow. For streams of values, neither callback form is ideal in a modern Kotlin API: expose Flow<Progress> for Kotlin and offer a callback adapter for Java.
  • Docs guidance. The official fun interface page suggests function types or aliases when "any function of this shape" is acceptable, and functional interfaces when the API carries contract or semantics beyond the shape.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Library public API
fun interface ProgressListener {
    fun onProgress(percent: Int)
    fun throttled(minDelta: Int): ProgressListener {          // evolvable helper (default method)
        var last = -minDelta
        return ProgressListener { p -> if (p - last >= minDelta) { last = p; onProgress(p) } }
    }
}

class Downloader {
    fun download(url: String, listener: ProgressListener) { listener.onProgress(100) }
}

// Kotlin caller: lambda via SAM conversion
fun kotlinCaller(d: Downloader) = d.download("u") { p -> println(p) }
// Java caller: d.download("u", p -> System.out.println(p));   // no Unit.INSTANCE, int not Integer

internal typealias Reducer<S> = (S, Action) -> S              // internal Kotlin-only: alias is fine
sealed interface Action

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing a typealias gives type safety. typealias UserId = String accepts any String. A value class does what people hoped (K2b).
  • Exposing function types in an SDK and later needing a second callback method, which forces a breaking change.
  • Choosing fun interface and then relying on lambda identity for unregistration (Q102).
  • Forgetting that Kotlin's stdlib-style higher-order inline functions should take function types. You can't inline a fun interface parameter in the same way.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can an inline function take a fun interface parameter and inline it? → No. Inlining applies to function-type parameters. A fun interface argument is an object passed normally.
  2. How would you migrate an existing (Int) -> Unit public API to a fun interface without breaking anyone? → Add the new overload taking ProgressListener, deprecate the old one with ReplaceWith, and keep the old one delegating. Watch for overload ambiguity at Kotlin lambda call sites: when both accept a lambda, the function-type overload is preferred. Verify with the binary-compatibility validator and a compile check.
  3. When is a full interface (not fun) right? → When there are several required callbacks (onSuccess/onError/onCancel). SAM sugar doesn't fit, and Kotlin callers use object :.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev picks function types "because they're idiomatic". The senior decides by caller population and lifespan, cites Java signatures, boxing, type-distinctness and evolvability, and has a migration path that respects binary compatibility.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An SDK's onEvent: (String, Map<String, Any>) -> Unit needed a third argument (timestamp). Every integrator had to change code. The v2 fun interface EventListener later gained onBatch as a default method with zero integrator breakage.

questions.promptHtml: What does tailrec do, what exactly qualifies as a tail call, and what do you do for recursion that isn't tail-recursive but is too deep for the stack?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you know the compiler transformation and its limits, and that you know deep-recursion alternatives (DeepRecursiveFunction, explicit stacks), which matter for parsers, tree walks and JSON or view hierarchies on Android's smaller thread stacks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: tailrec tells the compiler to rewrite self-recursion into a loop when the recursive call is the very last operation, meaning nothing remains to be done with its result. The function then uses constant stack and can't StackOverflowError. It must call itself directly in tail position, can't be open, and the tail call can't sit inside try/catch/finally. If no call qualifies, I get a warning, not an error, and the function stays recursive. For non-tail recursion, like a tree walk with two recursive calls, I use DeepRecursiveFunction (stable since Kotlin 1.7), which keeps the frames on the heap, or an explicit ArrayDeque stack.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Tail position: the call's result is returned as-is.
    • return go(n - 1, acc * n) is a tail call.
    • return n * fact(n - 1) is not, because a multiply happens after.
    • 1 + go(...), go(...) ?: 0, or a call followed by finally cleanup are not tail calls either.
  • The transformation:
tailrec fun gcd(a: Int, b: Int): Int = if (b == 0) a else gcd(b, a % b)

=> while (true) { if (b == 0) return a; val t = a % b; a = b; b = t }

Parameters are reassigned and control jumps back to the top. No new frame is pushed.

  • Restrictions:
    • Must be a direct self-call.
    • Mutual recursion (isEven/isOdd) isn't optimized.
    • Not allowed on open functions, since an override could change what the call means.
    • Not inside try/catch/finally.
    • Supported on JVM and Kotlin/Native per the docs.
    • Without a qualifying tail call the compiler warns ("a function is marked as tail-recursive but no tail calls are found") and still compiles. Treat that warning as an error.
  • Why stack depth matters on Android: the main thread stack is commonly around 8 MB, but background Threads and many thread pools use smaller default stacks (often about 1 MB on ART). A recursive JSON or AST walk that's fine in a JVM unit test can overflow on a device worker thread with a few thousand levels of nesting. I won't quote exact frame sizes. Measure with a test at the expected maximum depth.
  • DeepRecursiveFunction<T, R>: you write the recursion naturally with callRecursive(x). Under the hood it uses suspend-style continuations allocated on the heap, so depth is limited by heap, not stack. It costs allocation per call, so it's slower than a loop but safe.
  • Explicit stack: ArrayDeque<Node>-based iteration. It's the fastest and the most code, and the best choice when the hot path matters.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
tailrec fun indexOfFirst(xs: IntArray, pred: (Int) -> Boolean, i: Int = 0): Int = when {
    i >= xs.size -> -1
    pred(xs[i]) -> i
    else -> indexOfFirst(xs, pred, i + 1)                 // tail call -> loop
}

// NOT optimized: work after the call. The compiler warns because no tail calls are found.
tailrec fun badSum(n: Int): Long = if (n == 0) 0 else n + badSum(n - 1)

class Tree(val left: Tree?, val right: Tree?)

val depth = DeepRecursiveFunction<Tree?, Int> { t ->
    if (t == null) 0 else 1 + maxOf(callRecursive(t.left), callRecursive(t.right))
}

fun depthIterative(root: Tree?): Int {                     // explicit stack alternative
    if (root == null) return 0
    val stack = ArrayDeque<Pair<Tree, Int>>().apply { add(root to 1) }
    var max = 0
    while (stack.isNotEmpty()) {
        val (n, d) = stack.removeLast()
        max = maxOf(max, d)
        n.left?.let { stack.add(it to d + 1) }
        n.right?.let { stack.add(it to d + 1) }
    }
    return max
}
// usage: depth(root)   // operator invoke on DeepRecursiveFunction

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Marking a function tailrec and ignoring the warning. It's still recursive and still overflows.
  • Wrapping the tail call in try for error handling, which silently disables the optimization.
  • Assuming the JVM does tail-call elimination itself. It doesn't. Only the Kotlin compiler rewrite helps.
  • Testing deep recursion only in JVM unit tests with a different stack size than device worker threads.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is tailrec faster than a loop? → It is a loop after compilation, the same performance. Its value is expressing an accumulator-style algorithm clearly.
  2. Can a suspend function be tailrec? → The modifier is permitted. Whether a suspension in the chain matters depends on the function, and I'd verify in decompiled bytecode rather than assume. In practice suspend recursion is better written as a loop.
  3. How would you handle 50k-deep nested JSON from an untrusted server? → Don't recurse unbounded at all. Use a streaming parser (JsonReader) with an explicit depth cap. This is a trust-boundary DoS concern, not just a stack concern.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE dev says "tailrec optimizes recursion". The senior defines tail position precisely, lists the restrictions (open, try/finally, mutual recursion, warning-not-error), knows the JVM doesn't do TCO, and reaches for DeepRecursiveFunction or an explicit stack with Android thread-stack reasoning.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A comment-thread renderer recursed into replies on Dispatchers.Default. One viral thread with reply chains around 3,000 deep crashed with StackOverflowError on worker threads. A DeepRecursiveFunction flattening pass fixed it with no visible slowdown at p95.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app with 2.1M DAU sees OOM crashes rise from 0.05% to 0.4% of sessions over two releases, concentrated on 3 GB RAM devices (about 40% of the user base). Users rotate or leave the article screen often. Crashlytics shows java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 4194316 byte allocation in Glide decode paths, so the team suspects Glide caching (red herring). A heap dump from a debug build shows 14 ArticleActivity instances retained. Relevant code added two releases ago:

object ConnectivityMonitor {
    private val listeners = mutableListOf<(Boolean) -> Unit>()
    fun addListener(l: (Boolean) -> Unit) { listeners += l }
    fun removeListener(l: (Boolean) -> Unit) { listeners -= l }
}

class ArticleActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var binding: ActivityArticleBinding
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        binding = ActivityArticleBinding.inflate(layoutInflater)
        setContentView(binding.root)
        ConnectivityMonitor.addListener { online -> binding.offlineBanner.isVisible = !online }
    }
    override fun onDestroy() {
        ConnectivityMonitor.removeListener { online -> binding.offlineBanner.isVisible = !online }
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosing and fixing this, and explain what exactly the lambda retains.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Glide is caching too many bitmaps, reduce the memory cache." Or "Use a WeakReference to the Activity inside the lambda." The first treats the symptom location (where the allocation failed) as the cause. The second patches one capture while the listener list still grows forever.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Did OOMs start with the release that introduced ConnectivityMonitor? That correlates the cause.
    • Does the retained-Activity count grow with rotations? That confirms a per-instance leak.
    • Are other screens using the same monitor?
    • What's the large-heap/maxMemory on affected devices? That explains the device skew.
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Server-side flag the offline banner feature off if it's gated.
    • Otherwise ship a hotfix storing the listener (below).
    • Glide memory cache tweaks only move where the OOM happens, so I'd skip them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Every ArticleActivity registers a lambda in a process-lifetime singleton and never successfully unregisters. Each lambda strongly retains the Activity through its capture, and with it the whole view tree and its bitmaps.
    2. Glide caches too much: no, Glide's memory cache is bounded, and the dump shows Activities retained via ConnectivityMonitor.
    3. binding leaking through some other holder: possible, but it's reached through the same path.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • LeakCanary in debug: rotate 5×, and the trace reads ConnectivityMonitor.INSTANCE → listeners (ArrayList) → [i] ArticleActivity$onCreate$1 → this$0 / receiver ArticleActivity → mDestroyed = true.
    • Android Studio Memory Profiler: heap dump, filter ArticleActivity, and check its count against rotation count.
    • A debugger on ConnectivityMonitor.listeners.size, which grows by one per rotation.
  5. Root cause (mechanical):
    • The lambda references binding, a member property, so it captures this (the Activity). A Kotlin lambda only captures what it uses. If it had used nothing from the Activity, it wouldn't capture it, unlike a Java anonymous inner class, which always holds the outer instance. Here it uses binding, so it holds the Activity, and the Activity holds its window, views and drawables.
    • removeListener receives a new lambda object. listeners -= l uses equals, which is identity for lambdas, so nothing is removed. Every rotation adds one permanent entry. After 14 rotations, 14 Activities with full view trees: at roughly 15–25 MB each with article images, 14 × ~20 MB ≈ 280 MB, which exceeds a typical 256 MB per-app heap on a 3 GB device. The next 4 MB bitmap decode in Glide fails, which is why the stack points at Glide.
  6. Fix:
// Short-term: store the instance and pair register/unregister with a lifecycle callback
class ArticleActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var binding: ActivityArticleBinding
    private val onConnectivity: (Boolean) -> Unit = { online -> binding.offlineBanner.isVisible = !online }

    override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); ConnectivityMonitor.addListener(onConnectivity) }
    override fun onStop() { ConnectivityMonitor.removeListener(onConnectivity); super.onStop() }
}

// Long-term: the monitor exposes state, and the UI collects it lifecycle-aware
// (callbackFlow + stateIn in C10/F5; repeatOnLifecycle details in F5)
class ConnectivityRepository(/* ConnectivityManager */) {
    val online: kotlinx.coroutines.flow.StateFlow<Boolean> = TODO("callbackFlow { ... }.stateIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), true)")
}

Using onStart/onStop instead of onCreate/onDestroy also stops updates to an invisible screen. 7. Prevention:

  • LeakCanary in debug and QA builds, plus a CI instrumentation test that rotates 10× and runs LeakAssertions.assertNoLeaks() (leakcanary-android-instrumentation).
  • A review rule: no MutableList<(T) -> Unit> listener registries in singletons. Expose Flow instead.
  • Track OOM rate per device-RAM bucket in Crashlytics custom keys.
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I would not use WeakReference inside the lambda. The list still grows unboundedly, and weak refs hide lifecycle bugs instead of fixing them.
    • I would not increase largeHeap. It delays the crash and slows GC.
    • I would not make the listener registry hold weak references to lambdas. A lambda held only weakly gets collected immediately and silently stops working.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• If the lambda were { online -> Log.d("x", "$online") }, would it leak the Activity? → No. It captures nothing from the Activity, so it's a non-capturing lambda and may even be a singleton. The registry still grows, but without the heavy objects.
  • What if you used binding.offlineBanner::setVisibility-style bound references? → It captures the View, which references its Context (the Activity). It leaks just the same.
  • Same pattern in a Fragment using binding? → Worse. It leaks the view hierarchy past onDestroyView as well. Register against viewLifecycleOwner (C7).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An app-wide "theme changed" callback registry held lambdas from every screen ever opened. OOMs clustered on low-RAM devices after long sessions and were blamed on the image loader for a quarter. A single LeakCanary trace pointed straight at the singleton list, and replacing it with a StateFlow closed the issue.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes Glide or reaches for largeHeap/WeakReference without finding the registry.
  • Hire: identifies the capture of this via binding, the failed removal due to a new lambda instance, and stores the listener with paired lifecycle callbacks.
  • Strong hire: explains the Kotlin-vs-Java capture difference, does the heap math linking the leak to the Glide-located OOM, verifies with a LeakCanary trace and an automated leak test, and moves the API to a lifecycle-collected StateFlow.

questions.contextHtml:
A profile screen shows a tooltip 3 seconds after opening. Since the release that added it, the profile flow's crash rate went from 0.02% to 0.3% (about 1,900 crashes/day at 640k daily profile opens). It happens mostly to users who tap back within 3 seconds. A ViewBinding Gradle plugin bump in the same release is suspected (red herring). Crashlytics:

java.lang.NullPointerException
    at com.app.profile.ProfileFragment.getBinding(ProfileFragment.kt:21)
    at com.app.profile.ProfileFragment$onViewCreated$$inlined$afterDelay$1.run(ViewExt.kt:9)
    at android.os.Handler.handleCallback(Handler.java:958)
    at android.os.Looper.loopOnce(Looper.java:205)
// ViewExt.kt
inline fun Fragment.afterDelay(delayMs: Long, crossinline block: () -> Unit) {
    view?.postDelayed({ block() }, delayMs)                       // line 9
}

// ProfileFragment.kt
class ProfileFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_profile) {
    private var _binding: FragmentProfileBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!                          // line 21
    private val viewModel: ProfileViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentProfileBinding.bind(view)
        afterDelay(3_000) {
            binding.tooltip.isVisible = true
            viewModel.markTooltipShown()
        }
    }
    override fun onDestroyView() {
        _binding = null
        super.onDestroyView()
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every bug in this helper and its usage, explain why crossinline is involved, and rewrite it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Replace _binding!! with _binding?." That suppresses the crash. The Runnable still fires after the view is gone, markTooltipShown() still runs for a tooltip that was never shown, and the Fragment is still retained for 3 seconds. Another weak answer: "Remove crossinline." That doesn't compile.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is afterDelay used elsewhere? I'd grep it, because every caller has the same lifetime bug.
    • Does markTooltipShown() persist state? If so, we're also corrupting data, not just crashing.
    • Is the ViewBinding plugin bump in the stack? No: the frame is our $$inlined$afterDelay$1, which rules out the red herring.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the helper itself, so all call sites are fixed at once. If the tooltip is behind a remote flag, turn it off in the meantime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. The posted Runnable outlives the Fragment's view. View.postDelayed puts it in the main Looper's queue, and nothing removes it in onDestroyView, so it runs after _binding = null.
    2. Back-press timing: confirmed by the "within 3 s" pattern.
    3. The plugin bump: no change in the binding getter.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Unit-test the repro with Robolectric: launch the fragment, move it to DESTROYED with FragmentScenario.moveToState, then ShadowLooper.idleFor(3, SECONDS) and watch it crash.
    • Manual repro: open the screen, press back at 1 s.
    • Decompile to see the synthetic ProfileFragment$onViewCreated$$inlined$afterDelay$1 class implementing Runnable with a captured this$0.
  5. Root cause, and the role of crossinline:
    • afterDelay is inline, but block is called inside another lambda (the Runnable) that executes later, in a different stack frame.
    • A lambda inlined there could contain a non-local return from onViewCreated, which is impossible once that frame has finished. So the compiler forces crossinline, which forbids non-local returns (only return@afterDelay is allowed).
