    • Crucially, crossinline doesn't make the lambda "safe" or lifecycle-aware. It copies the block's body into a new synthetic Runnable class per call site. That class captures the Fragment, and here also binding through the getter.
    • The bugs:
# Bug Effect
1 Runnable not tied to the view lifecycle; never removed NPE after onDestroyView; also runs on a detached view after a config change
2 No handle returned, so callers cannot removeCallbacks The leak can't be fixed at the call site
3 view?. silently no-ops if called before onCreateView Tooltip silently never shows when the helper is called from onCreate
4 Runnable captures the Fragment for up to 3 s after destroy Short-lived retention; LeakCanary may flag it at its watch time
5 markTooltipShown() side effect runs even if the UI update can't happen Tooltip marked as seen but never shown; wrong analytics/state
6 Inline + crossinline creates a synthetic class per call site Minor code-size cost multiplied across call sites (Q109)
  1. Fix:
// Not inline: no reified type, nothing to gain from inlining. The lifecycle owns the timer.
fun Fragment.afterDelay(delayMs: Long, block: () -> Unit): Job =
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {       // throws ISE if called with no view: fail fast
        delay(delayMs)
        block()                                       // never runs after onDestroyView: the Job is cancelled
    }

class ProfileFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_profile) {
    private var _binding: FragmentProfileBinding? = null
    private val binding get() = _binding!!
    private val viewModel: ProfileViewModel by viewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        _binding = FragmentProfileBinding.bind(view)
        afterDelay(3_000) {
            binding.tooltip.isVisible = true
            viewModel.markTooltipShown()              // only when actually shown
        }
    }
    override fun onDestroyView() { _binding = null; super.onDestroyView() }
}

If it must stay Handler-based (no coroutines in that module), return the Runnable, store it, and call view.removeCallbacks(r) in onDestroyView, or register a DefaultLifecycleObserver on viewLifecycleOwner that removes it in onDestroy. 7. Prevention:

  • Ban postDelayed from Fragment code via a lint/detekt rule (ForbiddenMethodCall on View.postDelayed/Handler.postDelayed in ui packages).
  • Robolectric tests that destroy the view mid-delay.
  • Review checklist: "every deferred callback names its owner lifecycle".
  1. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't "fix" it with _binding?. alone or if (isAdded) checks scattered at call sites.
    • I wouldn't keep the function inline. Inlining helps when it removes a lambda allocation on a hot path or enables reified. Here it buys nothing and multiplies classes.
    • The viewLifecycleOwner ISE when there is no view is a deliberate fail-fast.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why crossinline and not noinline? → noinline would pass the lambda as a real object into the Runnable, which also compiles and avoids the per-call-site copy. crossinline keeps inlining the body into the Runnable but bans non-local returns. Either way, the lifetime bug remains.
  • Would lifecycleScope (the Fragment's, not the view's) be fine? → No. It lives until the Fragment's onDestroy, which on the back stack is long after onDestroyView. The same NPE comes back when the fragment is on the back stack with its view destroyed (C7 covers this).
  • What if block is a suspend lambda? → Then the helper takes suspend () -> Unit, with the same structure. It works because launch provides the coroutine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared debounceClick inline helper used crossinline plus postDelayed. It was copied into about 300 call sites before anyone noticed it fired after navigation. Replacing it with a lifecycle-scoped, non-inline helper fixed a crash cluster and cut roughly 300 synthetic classes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests ?. on the binding, or can't say why crossinline is required.
  • Hire: identifies the un-removable Runnable outliving the view, explains crossinline's non-local-return rule, and rewrites with viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.
  • Strong hire: lists the side-effect and silent no-op bugs, knows viewLifecycleOwner vs lifecycleScope, removes inline with a justification, and adds a lint rule and destroy-mid-delay tests.

questions.contextHtml:
An e-commerce app (about 14M installs, 35% on low-end devices with 2–3 GB RAM) adds a "perf improvement" PR that made the analytics helper inline "to avoid lambda allocations". Next release:

  • Release APK goes from 18.2 MB to 20.1 MB.
  • Dex files go from 3 to 4.
  • Cold start p50 on low-end devices goes from 1.42 s to 1.49 s.
  • Macrobenchmark startup p95 is +60 ms.

The team blames a new image library added in the same release (red herring: it's 180 KB). The helper has about 2,300 call sites:

inline fun <reified T : Any> Analytics.track(
    event: String,
    crossinline props: MutableMap<String, Any?>.() -> Unit
) {
    if (!sampler.shouldSample(event)) return
    executor.execute {
        try {
            val map = HashMap<String, Any?>()
            map.props()
            map["screen"] = T::class.java.simpleName
            map["ts"] = clock.now()
            map["session"] = session.id
            // ... ~35 more lines: enrichment, PII scrubbing, JSON encoding, batching
            queue.offer(encoder.encode(event, map))
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            logger.e("track failed", e)
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain the size and startup regression mechanically, quantify it, and redesign the API.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Inline is always faster because there's no lambda. The size increase must be the new image library, so enable minifyEnabled." It doesn't understand that inline copies the body into every call site and that crossinline inside a Runnable generates a class per call site. R8 is already on.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Was track previously non-inline? That gives the before/after baseline.
    • Why does it need reified? Only T::class.java.simpleName.
    • What were the actual allocation savings measured? Usually nobody measured.
    • Is the APK diff concentrated in dex? A diff tool tells us.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the PR, since it's self-contained. No user-facing behaviour depends on it. Ship the redesign in the next train.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Inline body duplication across 2,300 call sites, plus a synthetic Runnable class per call site for the crossinline block.
    2. The image library: diff shows 180 KB, which is too small.
    3. R8 config change: check mapping.txt and the R8 version. Unchanged.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • diffuse diff old.apk new.apk shows dex size, class count and method count deltas.
    • Android Studio APK Analyzer on classes*.dex: count *$$inlined$track$* classes.
    • apkanalyzer dex packages --defined-only.
    • Decompile one call site to see the copied body.
    • Macrobenchmark StartupTimingMetric before and after the revert, on a low-end device.
  5. Root cause and math:
    • inline copies the whole function body, including the enrichment code, into every caller.
    • Because props is crossinline and used inside executor.execute { }, each call site also gets its own synthetic Runnable class that captures props's environment and contains the copied 40-line body.
    • Rough numbers, which I'd confirm with diffuse:
per call site: ~550 B dex code for the inlined body + ~150 B class/method/field overhead ≈ 700 B
2,300 call sites × 700 B ≈ 1.61 MB  (matches most of the +1.9 MB APK; rest is string/proto refs)
new classes: ~2,300 synthetic Runnables; methods: ≥ 2 each (ctor + run) ≈ 4,600+ new methods
  • Startup impact: more dex to map and verify, a 4th dex file, more classes loaded for screens hit at startup, and a larger baseline-profile footprint. Every first-launched screen pays to load its own copy of the analytics logic instead of sharing one hot, JIT/AOT-compiled method.
  • The "saving" was one small lambda allocation per event. Most call sites' props lambdas would allocate a short-lived object, a few dozen bytes, which young-gen GC handles trivially.
  • A second smell: for a public inline function, sampler, executor, clock, queue and encoder must all be public (or @PublishedApi internal), so internals leaked into the API.
  1. Fix: a thin inline shim and a single non-inline body.
inline fun <reified T : Any> Analytics.track(
    event: String,
    props: MutableMap<String, Any?>.() -> Unit = {}
) {
    if (!shouldSample(event)) return                         // cheap check stays inline
    trackImpl(event, T::class.java.simpleName, HashMap<String, Any?>().apply(props))
}

class Analytics internal constructor(/* deps */) {
    @PublishedApi internal fun shouldSample(event: String): Boolean = TODO()
    @PublishedApi internal fun trackImpl(event: String, screen: String, map: MutableMap<String, Any?>) {
        executor.execute { /* the 40 lines, compiled ONCE */ }
    }
    private val executor: java.util.concurrent.Executor = TODO()
}
  • Each call site now inlines about 4 instructions plus its own props body, which is the caller's own code anyway. There is no per-call-site Runnable class.
  • The props map is now built on the caller's thread before the hop. I'd check that the props lambdas are cheap, which they are: key/value puts. The original's laziness only mattered for expensive props, and those are rare.
  • If reified weren't needed, I'd drop inline completely and take screen: String or KClass<*>.
  1. Prevention:
    • A CI size gate: diffuse or the Gradle size-reporting plugin comparing against main, failing on more than +200 KB dex without a label.
    • A detekt rule or review checklist: public inline functions need a reason (reified, lambda on a measured hot path, non-local return) and a body under about 10 lines.
    • Macrobenchmark startup in CI on a low-end device profile.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't rely on R8 to "dedupe" the copies. R8 does some class merging of synthetic classes, but the bodies differ per call site, so most can't merge. I wouldn't count on it without measuring.
    • I wouldn't remove reified by making callers pass this::class. That's API churn for no gain.
    • I wouldn't move the props building back into the background lambda via noinline. That reintroduces an allocation and a capture per call, which is fine but buys nothing measurable here.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does inline increase method count? → An inlined body adds no method by itself, since it goes into the caller. The method explosion came from crossinline lambdas inside nested lambdas generating classes per call site.
  • When is a large inline justified? → Rarely: stdlib-style tiny combinators (let, map), reified helpers that are thin shims, or a measured hot loop where a lambda allocation per iteration shows in a profile.
  • What about ABI? → A public inline body is compiled into consumers. Changing it requires consumers to recompile, and it can't reference private API (K3a covers the ABI rules in depth).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A logging inline fun d(msg: () -> String) helper with an inlined formatting body was copied into roughly 5,000 call sites. Moving the body into a @PublishedApi internal function, leaving only if (enabled) logImpl(msg()) inline, removed about 900 KB of dex.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes inline is free or faster, blames the image library, or wants to "turn on R8".
  • Hire: explains body duplication and per-call-site classes from crossinline, verifies with an APK diff, proposes a thin shim plus @PublishedApi internal implementation.
  • Strong hire: quantifies size and method impact with math, links it to startup (dex loading, baseline profiles), discusses eager vs lazy props trade-offs, notes the leaked-internals smell, and adds CI size and startup gates.

questions.contextHtml:
The platform team publishes com.acme:analytics-core as an AAR. Six app teams depend on it, plus a prebuilt partner chat SDK compiled against analytics-core:3.4. In 3.5 a developer "harmlessly" added a parameter with a default:

// 3.4
object Analytics { fun logEvent(name: String, params: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap()) { /* ... */ } }
// 3.5
object Analytics { fun logEvent(name: String, params: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap(), sampleRate: Double = 1.0) { /* ... */ } }

The main app bumped to 3.5. Gradle resolved the chat SDK's transitive 3.4 to 3.5 (highest version wins). The app compiled cleanly, all unit tests passed, and the release went out. Within hours:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: No static method logEvent$default(Lcom/acme/analytics/Analytics;Ljava/lang/String;Ljava/util/Map;ILjava/lang/Object;)V
  in class Lcom/acme/analytics/Analytics; or its super classes
    at com.partner.chat.ChatSession.open(ChatSession.kt:88)

The crash hits 6% of chat-opening sessions, about 0.9% of all sessions. The on-call engineer first added -keep class com.acme.analytics.** { *; } assuming R8 stripped the method (red herring). It didn't help.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "R8 removed the method, add keep rules," or "The partner SDK must recompile." The first is disproven by the keep rule not helping. The second is unrealistic for a prebuilt third-party binary, and it misses that adding a defaulted parameter is a binary-breaking change in Kotlin.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which artifacts were compiled against 3.4 and are consumed as binaries? The partner SDK, possibly internal prebuilt modules from a binary cache.
    • Is there a .api dump for analytics-core?
    • Does dependency resolution show 3.4 → 3.5? ./gradlew :app:dependencies --configuration releaseRuntimeClasspath would tell us.
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Option A, fastest with low risk: ship analytics-core:3.5.1 restoring the old binary signature (below) and rebuild the app.
    • Option B, if the release train is slow: force analytics-core:3.4 via strictly constraints, if nothing in the app needs 3.5 API yet.
    • Also halt the staged rollout immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. A binary signature change: callers compiled against 3.4 call logEvent$default(Analytics, String, Map, int, Object), which no longer exists.
    2. R8 stripping: ruled out. The keep rule didn't help, and javap on the 3.5 class shows the method was never generated.
    3. A partner SDK bug: no, it's calling exactly what it was compiled against.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • javap -p (or the IDE bytecode viewer) on Analytics.class from both AARs.
      • 3.4 has logEvent(String, Map) and logEvent$default(Analytics, String, Map, int, Object).
      • 3.5 has logEvent(String, Map, double) and logEvent$default(Analytics, String, Map, double, int, Object).
    • The partner SDK's bytecode call site references the 3.4 synthetic.
  5. Root cause (mechanical):
    • In Kotlin, default values are not overloads. A Kotlin caller that omitted params compiled to a call to the static synthetic logEvent$default(...) with a bitmask (Q096).
    • Adding a parameter changes both the real method's descriptor and the $default descriptor. Source compatibility is preserved, because every Kotlin caller still compiles, which is why our app was green. Binary compatibility is broken for anything compiled against the old version.
    • Java callers of logEvent(String, Map) would break the same way.
    • Nothing caught it because every module in our repo was recompiled from source. Only the prebuilt binary called the old descriptor, and only on the chat path, which our smoke tests didn't open.
  6. Fix:
object Analytics {
    fun logEvent(name: String, params: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap(), sampleRate: Double = 1.0) { /* ... */ }

    // Restores the 3.4 ABI: both logEvent(String, Map) and its logEvent$default(..., int, Object).
    // HIDDEN keeps it in bytecode but invisible to Kotlin source, so no overload ambiguity.
    @Deprecated("Binary compatibility with 3.4", level = DeprecationLevel.HIDDEN)
    fun logEvent(name: String, params: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap()) = logEvent(name, params, 1.0)
}
  • Why not just add @JvmOverloads to the new function? It would regenerate logEvent(String, Map), which fixes Java callers and Kotlin callers that passed all arguments. But it does not regenerate the old logEvent$default(Analytics, String, Map, int, Object) that Kotlin callers omitting params use. The hidden overload with its own defaults restores both.
  • Long-term: an API-evolution policy. New optional knobs go into a parameter object or builder (EventOptions), or into a new overload, never as appended parameters to published functions without keeping the old signature.
  1. Prevention:
    • Adopt the Kotlin binary-compatibility-validator Gradle plugin (apiDump/apiCheck) on every published module. Its .api file lists synthetic $default methods, so this PR would have shown a removed line and failed CI. Recent Kotlin Gradle Plugin versions also ship an experimental built-in ABI validation; I'd check its status for our KGP version before relying on it.
    • Semver discipline: a removed ABI entry requires a major version.
    • A consumer-side test that runs the partner SDK's entry points (an instrumentation smoke test opening chat).
    • Dependency-resolution review: flag transitive upgrades of libraries that prebuilt binaries depend on.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do:
    • I wouldn't add blanket -keep rules. They don't address the cause and bloat the APK.
    • I wouldn't pin everyone to 3.4 forever.
    • I wouldn't use @JvmOverloads as the "compat fix" for Kotlin callers, for the reason above.
    • I accept that DeprecationLevel.HIDDEN overloads accumulate. I'd remove them at the next major version with release notes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is changing a default value (emptyMap() to mapOf("v" to 2)) binary-safe? → Yes for non-inline functions. The value is computed inside the library's $default body, so old binaries pick up the new value without recompiling. That can be a behavioural break, though.
  • What else in Kotlin breaks binaries silently? → Adding a property to a data class's primary constructor changes copy, componentN and the constructor signature (see K2a). Changing a top-level function's file changes its FileNameKt facade class unless @file:JvmName is used (K11). Changing a public inline function body only takes effect when consumers recompile.
  • How would you design logEvent to evolve without this pain? → fun logEvent(name: String, options: EventOptions = EventOptions.Default), with EventOptions being a class whose fields can be added with defaults. Avoid a data class for it if it's published, for the reasons in the previous follow-up.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A design-system AAR added contentDescription: String? = null to a public @Composable function. Feature modules served from a remote build cache, compiled against the old version, crashed with NoSuchMethodError on staging. The binary-compatibility validator went into CI the same week and caught four more such changes that quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: insists on R8 keep rules, or thinks default params are binary-safe because the "code still compiles".
  • Hire: explains the $default synthetic signature change and source vs binary compatibility, and restores the old signature with a hidden deprecated overload.
  • Strong hire: explains why @JvmOverloads doesn't restore the $default entry point, sets up the binary-compatibility validator and semver policy, proposes an options-object API, and lists other silent ABI breakers.
